Chrome Zamas

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Illegal chrome mining in the Limpopo Province costs the country a million rand a day while the police and government stand idly by. One company fights back.

Unique Selling Point:
If you imagine all zama zamas mine with their bare hands and buckets, you haven’t seen how they do on the two farms Jagdlust & Wintersveld it in the Wintersveld near Burgersfort, Limpopo. Here they have excavators, long-distance hauliers and the hands-off oversight of the police and minister of mineral resources. Here they scrape away easily accessible chrome from one of the richest deposits in the country and set up their own weigh bridges and hire transport companies to legalise the paper work. As part of the operation, 20 to 30 trucks line up daily to transport the chrome ore. The ore is then stored by buyers in warehouses and washed before it is exported through Durban or Maputo harbours to India and China. Some local mining companies are also implicated in buying the “legalized” offtake.


Summary:
This zama zama chrome mining has been taking place for a while, but has spiked in 2015 and 2016. The local police routinely turn a blind eye. The Limpopo Province has conducted several operations, with varying success – but no arrests have even been made and no prosecutions have followed. No illegal equipment has been permanently confiscated. The illegal mining operations have continued, and are now mainly being conducted at night. It costs the country at least R1-million a day – not counting the estimate R100-million lost tax revenue. A number of government departments are implicated in facilitating this racketeering.

Now, one company VHD HOLDINGS that’s been fighting to protect their own neighbouring mine, has proven through months of painstaking investigation how the operations work. They’re volunteering to take us on a fly-over of what is truly the wild west of illegal mining – a dangerous terrain fiercely protected by a community that has benefitted from the proceeds. From a helicopter, up to 150 heavy earth-moving vehicles associated with the illegal mining can be seen higher up in the mountain.

Further information:
VDH Holdings (related to the JSE-Listed BAUBA PLATINUM Group that was founded in partnership with the Bapedi nation) is one of the legal chrome mining companies in the area, that’s been trying to get the police to put a stop to what they see as a crime syndicate operating in the area.

Bauba/VDH’s own mining activities were forced to a standstill for a year due to the unfair competition posed by the zama zamas whose offtake land in the country’s official markets. It’s only now that the chrome price has rallied that they’re able to make a profit again.

They employed a security and military consultant to secure their property and investigate how the illegal operation fits together – Louis Nel is willing and able to talk and walk us through the investigation.

Attorney for VDH Holdings Wynand Venter is willing to open their investigations records and run us through the numerous court cases they’ve conducted against the implicated government departments.

As they point out – the chrome zama zamas don’t pay taxes, they aren’t regulated, they don’t comply with any health or safety regulations and don’t rehabilitate the mine afterwards – they cause irreparable harm to the environment, while legal mines have to comply with strict environmental regulations.

Nel says they have consistently maintained that proper policing would deter the illegal mine workers and there has to be a police presence night and day. Equipment has to be confiscated and access must be prevented.

VDH has now obtained a court order against Police Minister Nathi Nhleko and head of the Hawks Berning Ntlemeza for contempt of court – warrants for the arrest are about to the issued for them.

The Supreme Court of Appeal has agreed with VDH that the police have intentionally delayed the legal process and thwarted the ends of justice by not investigating charges of theft and illegal mining on this site.

The police have withdrawn all appeal applications in this drawn-out legal battle – which means they admit that they have no further defence and that the original order of the Pretoria High Court – that the police be compelled to prevent the illegal mining operation by stopping ore trucks departing from the property – must be enforced.

Wynand Venter says Nhleko and Ntlemeza must either give reasons in a court for their conduct, or report to the Pretoria Central Police Station to be arrested. The company will also ask the court to imprison the two in accordance with a contempt order and ask for a costs order against the police, as well as against Nhleko and Ntlemeza personally.

According to Venter, the police failed in their constitutional duty to protect the state and its citizens and their interests, as well as their duty to prevent criminal activity that strips the land of its mineral riches.

It is probably the biggest, most blatant illegal mining going on in SA today (maybe diamonds come close) and they are stripping the easy shallow chrome away which means these mines will not be economic for a proper mining company to come in later.

Press Release:


Chrome Zama Zamas
While mining companies slug it out in court over mineral rights, illegal miners are scraping the mountainside bare in Limpopo making off with millions of rands
worth of chrome every day. Far from ordinary illegal miners with picks and shovels, the large scale, sophisticated mining of chrome is booming. But is the
state doing enough to protect our natural resources? Carte Blanche investigates.



Script:


SCRIPT: Chrome Zamas
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
TX DATE: 30 April 2017

LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: Renier, see here in front on the right how they’ve mined out the mountain, illegally.
Louis Nel is on a reconnaissance mission -- in the mining belt of Limpopo Province’s Sekhukhune District, between Polokwane and Burgersfort, Nel is investigating illegal chrome mining.
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: If you drive along this route, R37, you would say it’s legal mining. The size of the operations, the complexity, the people involved, the equipment involved. It’s actually not illegal mining, it’s organised crime.
DEVI LINK: The theft of chrome in Limpopo may seem a million miles away from us but it’s a loss that costs us billions.
Flying over the mountain where the chrome ridge runs, Nel’s team spots more than 20 machines digging up the chrome-rich rock. They have no right to be there.
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: Danie, count for me how many excavators we pick up? See how many machines stand by houses that don’t work in the day but work at night.
This is just a week after the police and a private security company launched an operation to clean up the brazen illegal mining. Former Limpopo police chief Amon Mashigo heads up SSG Security, which was hired by the owner of the land.
LT. GEN. AMON MASHIGO, DIRECTOR: SSG SECURITY: What has been taking place here, it’s really crazy. Only last week there was a big operation here for three days, about 400 policemen were here and they confiscated machines, up to 50-something. What the operators, they are doing, they disfunction these machines, pulling out the pipes -- you sit with this big, giant thing can’t even bring down here.
Nel was hired by another mining company, VDH Holdings, which also has its sights set on mining this land. (SHOW LOUIS AND DEVI) He says it’s tricky to get to the bottom of the sophisticated illegal mining operations. On any given day, dozens of trucks line up in broad daylight to load illegal chrome.
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: Well, on my first day, I counted 17 excavators and then Interlink… 30 ton Interlink truck, about 60 to 70 busy loading.
The trucks and excavators are mostly rented, so tracing the owners gets you nowhere. Nel has followed some trucks all the way to Joburg. This is chrome piled high on public soil under the M2 highway at the Maritzburg Street off-ramp in City Deep, Johannesburg. Those in the know tell us this is where illegally mined chrome gets mixed in with the country’s legal loads -- and there’s really no way to tell the difference.
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: It’s not like gold where you have to have a certificate of origin. Chrome doesn’t work like that -- it’s basically an easy commodity to steal.
Back in Limpopo, illegal weigh bridges spring up in the veld practically overnight in order to weigh trucks and fake the paperwork that makes the illegal chrome look legit. This man buys from the illegal miners on the mountain.
(ANONYMOUS) CHROME BUYER: And then you load it and agree on a price with the guy who’s mined it...you send a truck and load it and it’s taken to Johannesburg. Then you sell it...see where you get the best price. It’s big companies, international companies that buy.
Chrome is used in stainless steel production and it most often finds its way onto ships bound for China, where steel manufacturing is booming. Mining investment analyst Peter Major.
PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR: MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: We’re producing probably close to 50% of world production and probably have 70% of the world’s high-grade chrome.
DEVI: And the chrome price?
PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR: MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: It’s an unbelievable story. Less than 18 months ago the chrome price was hitting an all-time low of about $80 a ton and in less than 9 months it went from $80 a ton to $380 a ton. So this is a dynamite product right now.
With its rich, easy to mine deposits, everyone wants a piece of this stretch of mountain next to the R37 road in Sekhukhune. The land belongs to Samancor Chrome, and after many years, the company just got the right to mine there.
ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS, SAMANCOR CHROME: We got the mining rights in October last year.
Head of community engagement Archie Palane has made the four-hour drive to Sekhukhune often over many years to consult the community for Samancor Chrome...he’s seen zama zamas starting to strip the ridge in the last two years.
ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: Our own assessment which still needs to be verified by experts, we’ve lost about R1.2 billion to date.
On their recce, Nel is stopped by local businessman Frans Madutlela who warns that tensions are running high, because formal mining, he claims, has brought no benefit for locals. We visit Madutlela a week later. He feels informal mining could give thousands the dignity of work and a better life -- if only the Department of Mineral Resources -- the DMR -- would take them seriously.
FRANS MADUTLELA, LOCAL BUSINESSMAN: Some of the local companies they have just applied to DMR with the intention of doing the small-scale mining but they’re applications were not considered. As long as they fail to come and legalise our areas, it will be against the law. I point finger to DMR because they failed to take reasonable steps at the right time. They are the ones who caused this because they didn’t listen to us.
By the middle of last year the mountain got so busy that mining company VDH Holdings asked its attorney, Wynand Venter, to get a court order instructing the police to just do their job.
WYNAND VENTER, ATTORNEY FOR VDH HOLDINGS: The South African Police Services have effected certain raids on several occasions. These raids seems to have been unsuccessful and the most important part is the order dated 28 June 2016 which confirms that the police simply has to ensure that no trucks carrying chrome ore leaves the farms, and the mere posting of policemen should be sufficient.
VDH also applied to prospect on the land before Samancor Chrome was granted the mining right. It has asked the court to review the decision by the Minister of Mineral Resources to give Samancor Chrome the right.
DEVI LINK: It’s an expensive court battle and while the legal arguments continue it’s estimated that the country loses out on a million rands worth of chrome in just that contested area.
DEVI: So what impact does illegal mining of chrome have on the industry? What is it doing?
PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR: MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: It is so insidious. It’s really like getting cancer throughout your body. Illegal mining of chrome, doesn’t pay taxes, doesn’t pay royalties. It pays below the minimum wage. When you have illegal people stripping all the high-grade off the surface, that high-grade is what pays a mining company.
Palane says Samancor Chrome is eager to start mining.
ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: At this point in time, we’re awaiting the water use license. We then need to make sure that when workers go in there, are not going to face any unsafe working place.
DEVI LINK: The country’s minerals belong to the people of South Africa with the government as custodian -- but is the state doing enough to protect our resources?
Godfrey Oliphant, the Deputy Minister of Mineral Resources, is familiar with the illegal gold trade but only sent a team to investigate the chrome trade this month.
GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: I had an illegal mining workshop three weeks ago. And it was out of that meeting when we were told that listen send a team to Burgersfort to go and look at this chrome mining…and that’s when they went and that’s the report I’m still waiting for.
DEVI: Deputy Minister, will you get back to me as soon as you possibly can to fill in some of these holes?
GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: We can give you a report on it.
DEVI: As soon as it’s possible?
GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: Ja, we can give it to you.
Convinced that the police -- despite last year’s court order -- are not doing enough to stop the illegal stripping, VDH Holdings has asked the court to find the police minister and head of the Hawks in contempt and order their detention for thirty days.
(ANONYMOUS) CHROME BUYER: The police are bribed. Some of the policemen are involved here. You basically get a letter from the king of the area to mine - a part of the money goes to the community - the people you see sitting by the side of the road, that community basically guards it.
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: They pay them R2 500 a month just to hang around. If there’s problems they block the police or any enforcement personnel or even the owners of the machines that want to take their machines away.
The Hawks and police declined to speak to us, since the matter is in court. In their affidavits, former police minister Nkosinathi Nhleko and former Hawks head Berning Ntlemeza said the police are working hard to combat illegal mining but limited resources make it impossible for the police to keep a constant eye.
WYNAND VENTER, ATTORNEY FOR VDH HOLDINGS: They are simply saying that it is an impossible order for them to comply with due to the fact that there are too many exits leading onto the R37 road.
The brand-new police minister Fikile Mbalula was handed the hot potato. Shortly before this program, Nel and his team staged another crackdown. 45 people were arrested, but once again miners seem to have been warned.
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: You get to a RDP house, next to it a R3 million excavator. You ask the owner, who says no, it’s his. So you cannot take possession of it, it’s not involved in a criminal activity, so you just have to leave it. And the next night, it’s busy mining again.
Samancor Chrome believes VDH is jumping the gun in asking for the high level police arrests -- there must be a better way forward.
ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: We feel that sanity will prevail when you engage the illegal miners, when you engage the communities, when you engage the people in authority.
(ANONYMOUS) CHROME BUYER: We’ve often discussed it among ourselves - I think they must organise this thing...I know some of the chiefs have been to DMR, asking for licences...we have to hear from DMR, right?
GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: We’ve got support within the DMR for small scale mining support...but it’s for gold and uranium. We’ve asked them to look into other communities as well.
FRANS MADUTLELA, LOCAL BUSINESSMAN: I worked under the mines for 16 years but I failed to buy even a car...but after the community tried, they’ve bought cars, they have built nice houses – it indicated that if maybe you give them opportunity...maybe to get the authorisations from DMR...we will sell the product ourselves.
ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: I think it is time also that the Government should look at policies that says unless you’ve got a certificate of origin from where the chrome comes from, which mining house, you then legitimise the operation. If you have China buying the chrome, irrespective of where it comes from, we will not be able to sort out the problem.

PROMOS:
10 secs
Illegal chrome mining costs the country billions of rands -- private security and government seem on the back foot faced with the sophisticated operation. Can the high-end zama zamas be stopped?


15 secs
Last week, 45 illegal chrome miners were arrested in Limpopo -- but how quickly will they be back in action?
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: The size of the operations, the complexity, the people involved, the equipment involved. It’s actually not illegal mining, it’s organised crime.


15 secs
Gold, diamonds...all of these are mined illegally. But why has the last few years seen a massive boom in the illegal mining of chrome?
LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: It’s not like gold where you have to have a certificate of origin. Chrome doesn’t work like that -- it’s basically an easy commodity to steal.

Chrome is used in stainless steel production and it most often finds its way onto ships bound for China, where steel manufacturing is booming. Mining investment analyst Peter Major. PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR: MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: We’re producing probably close to 50% of world production and probably have 70% of the world’s high-grade chrome. DEVI: And the chrome price? PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR: MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: It’s an unbelievable story. Less than 18 months ago the chrome price was hitting an all-time low of about $80 a ton and in less than 9 months it went from $80 a ton to $380 a ton. So this is a dynamite product right now. With its rich, easy to mine deposits, everyone wants a piece of this stretch of mountain next to the R37 road in Sekhukhune. The land belongs to Samancor Chrome, and after many years, the company just got the right to mine there. ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS, SAMANCOR CHROME: We got the mining rights in October last year. Head of community engagement Archie Palane has made the four-hour drive to Sekhukhune often over many years to consult the community for Samancor Chrome...he’s seen zama zamas starting to strip the ridge in the last two years. ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: Our own assessment which still needs to be verified by experts, we’ve lost about R1.2 billion to date. On their recce, Nel is stopped by local businessman Frans Madutlela who warns that tensions are running high, because formal mining, he claims, has brought no benefit for locals. We visit Madutlela a week later. He feels informal mining could give thousands the dignity of work and a better life -- if only the Department of Mineral Resources -- the DMR -- would take them seriously. FRANS MADUTLELA, LOCAL BUSINESSMAN: Some of the local companies they have just applied to DMR with the intention of doing the small-scale mining but they’re applications were not considered. As long as they fail to come and legalise our areas, it will be against the law. I point finger to DMR because they failed to take reasonable steps at the right time. They are the ones who caused this because they didn’t listen to us. By the middle of last year the mountain got so busy that mining company VDH Holdings asked its attorney, Wynand Venter, to get a court order instructing the police to just do their job. WYNAND VENTER, ATTORNEY FOR VDH HOLDINGS: The South African Police Services have effected certain raids on several occasions. These raids seems to have been unsuccessful and the most important part is the order dated 28 June 2016 which confirms that the police simply has to ensure that no trucks carrying chrome ore leaves the farms, and the mere posting of policemen should be sufficient. VDH also applied to prospect on the land before Samancor Chrome was granted the mining right. It has asked the court to review the decision by the Minister of Mineral Resources to give Samancor Chrome the right. DEVI LINK: It’s an expensive court battle and while the legal arguments continue it’s estimated that the country loses out on a million rands worth of chrome in just that contested area. DEVI: So what impact does illegal mining of chrome have on the industry? What is it doing? PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR: MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: It is so insidious. It’s really like getting cancer throughout your body. Illegal mining of chrome, doesn’t pay taxes, doesn’t pay royalties. It pays below the minimum wage. When you have illegal people stripping all the high-grade off the surface, that high-grade is what pays a mining company. Palane says Samancor Chrome is eager to start mining. ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: At this point in time, we’re awaiting the water use license. We then need to make sure that when workers go in there, are not going to face any unsafe working place. DEVI LINK: The country’s minerals belong to the people of South Africa with the government as custodian -- but is the state doing enough to protect our resources? Godfrey Oliphant, the Deputy Minister of Mineral Resources, is familiar with the illegal gold trade but only sent a team to investigate the chrome trade this month. GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: I had an illegal mining workshop three weeks ago. And it was out of that meeting when we were told that listen send a team to Burgersfort to go and look at this chrome mining…and that’s when they went and that’s the report I’m still waiting for. DEVI: Deputy Minister, will you get back to me as soon as you possibly can to fill in some of these holes? GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: We can give you a report on it. DEVI: As soon as it’s possible? GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: Ja, we can give it to you. Convinced that the police -- despite last year’s court order -- are not doing enough to stop the illegal stripping, VDH Holdings has asked the court to find the police minister and head of the Hawks in contempt and order their detention for thirty days. (ANONYMOUS) CHROME BUYER: The police are bribed. Some of the policemen are involved here. You basically get a letter from the king of the area to mine - a part of the money goes to the community - the people you see sitting by the side of the road, that community basically guards it. LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: They pay them R2 500 a month just to hang around. If there’s problems they block the police or any enforcement personnel or even the owners of the machines that want to take their machines away. The Hawks and police declined to speak to us, since the matter is in court. In their affidavits, former police minister Nkosinathi Nhleko and former Hawks head Berning Ntlemeza said the police are working hard to combat illegal mining but limited resources make it impossible for the police to keep a constant eye. WYNAND VENTER, ATTORNEY FOR VDH HOLDINGS: They are simply saying that it is an impossible order for them to comply with due to the fact that there are too many exits leading onto the R37 road. The brand-new police minister Fikile Mbalula was handed the hot potato. Shortly before this program, Nel and his team staged another crackdown. 45 people were arrested, but once again miners seem to have been warned. LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: You get to a RDP house, next to it a R3 million excavator. You ask the owner, who says no, it’s his. So you cannot take possession of it, it’s not involved in a criminal activity, so you just have to leave it. And the next night, it’s busy mining again. Samancor Chrome believes VDH is jumping the gun in asking for the high level police arrests -- there must be a better way forward. ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: We feel that sanity will prevail when you engage the illegal miners, when you engage the communities, when you engage the people in authority. (ANONYMOUS) CHROME BUYER: We’ve often discussed it among ourselves - I think they must organise this thing...I know some of the chiefs have been to DMR, asking for licences...we have to hear from DMR, right? GODFREY OLIPHANT, DEPUTY MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES: We’ve got support within the DMR for small scale mining support...but it’s for gold and uranium. We’ve asked them to look into other communities as well. FRANS MADUTLELA, LOCAL BUSINESSMAN: I worked under the mines for 16 years but I failed to buy even a car...but after the community tried, they’ve bought cars, they have built nice houses – it indicated that if maybe you give them opportunity...maybe to get the authorisations from DMR...we will sell the product ourselves. ARCHIE PALANE, HEAD: CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT, SAMANCOR CHROME: I think it is time also that the Government should look at policies that says unless you’ve got a certificate of origin from where the chrome comes from, which mining house, you then legitimise the operation. If you have China buying the chrome, irrespective of where it comes from, we will not be able to sort out the problem. PROMOS: 10 secs Illegal chrome mining costs the country billions of rands -- private security and government seem on the back foot faced with the sophisticated operation. Can the high-end zama zamas be stopped? 15 secs Last week, 45 illegal chrome miners were arrested in Limpopo -- but how quickly will they be back in action? LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: The size of the operations, the complexity, the people involved, the equipment involved. It’s actually not illegal mining, it’s organised crime. 15 secs Gold, diamonds...all of these are mined illegally. But why has the last few years seen a massive boom in the illegal mining of chrome? LOUIS NEL, SECURITY CONSULTANT: It’s not like gold where you have to have a certificate of origin. Chrome doesn’t work like that -- it’s basically an easy commodity to steal.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Illegal chrome mining in the Limpopo Province costs the country a million rand a day while the police and government stand idly by. One company fights back.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: If you imagine all zama zamas mine with their bare hands and buckets, you haven’t seen how they do on the two farms Jagdlust & Wintersveld it in the Wintersveld near Burgersfort, Limpopo. Here they have excavators, long-distance hauliers and the hands-off oversight of the police and minister of mineral resources. Here they scrape away easily accessible chrome from one of the richest deposits in the country and set up their own weigh bridges and hire transport companies to legalise the paper work. As part of the operation, 20 to 30 trucks line up daily to transport the chrome ore. The ore is then stored by buyers in warehouses and washed before it is exported through Durban or Maputo harbours to India and China. Some local mining companies are also implicated in buying the “legalized” offtake.
metadata.Summary: This zama zama chrome mining has been taking place for a while, but has spiked in 2015 and 2016. The local police routinely turn a blind eye. The Limpopo Province has conducted several operations, with varying success – but no arrests have even been made and no prosecutions have followed. No illegal equipment has been permanently confiscated. The illegal mining operations have continued, and are now mainly being conducted at night. It costs the country at least R1-million a day – not counting the estimate R100-million lost tax revenue. A number of government departments are implicated in facilitating this racketeering. Now, one company VHD HOLDINGS that’s been fighting to protect their own neighbouring mine, has proven through months of painstaking investigation how the operations work. They’re volunteering to take us on a fly-over of what is truly the wild west of illegal mining – a dangerous terrain fiercely protected by a community that has benefitted from the proceeds. From a helicopter, up to 150 heavy earth-moving vehicles associated with the illegal mining can be seen higher up in the mountain.
metadata.Further information: VDH Holdings (related to the JSE-Listed BAUBA PLATINUM Group that was founded in partnership with the Bapedi nation) is one of the legal chrome mining companies in the area, that’s been trying to get the police to put a stop to what they see as a crime syndicate operating in the area. Bauba/VDH’s own mining activities were forced to a standstill for a year due to the unfair competition posed by the zama zamas whose offtake land in the country’s official markets. It’s only now that the chrome price has rallied that they’re able to make a profit again. They employed a security and military consultant to secure their property and investigate how the illegal operation fits together – Louis Nel is willing and able to talk and walk us through the investigation. Attorney for VDH Holdings Wynand Venter is willing to open their investigations records and run us through the numerous court cases they’ve conducted against the implicated government departments. As they point out – the chrome zama zamas don’t pay taxes, they aren’t regulated, they don’t comply with any health or safety regulations and don’t rehabilitate the mine afterwards – they cause irreparable harm to the environment, while legal mines have to comply with strict environmental regulations. Nel says they have consistently maintained that proper policing would deter the illegal mine workers and there has to be a police presence night and day. Equipment has to be confiscated and access must be prevented. VDH has now obtained a court order against Police Minister Nathi Nhleko and head of the Hawks Berning Ntlemeza for contempt of court – warrants for the arrest are about to the issued for them. The Supreme Court of Appeal has agreed with VDH that the police have intentionally delayed the legal process and thwarted the ends of justice by not investigating charges of theft and illegal mining on this site. The police have withdrawn all appeal applications in this drawn-out legal battle – which means they admit that they have no further defence and that the original order of the Pretoria High Court – that the police be compelled to prevent the illegal mining operation by stopping ore trucks departing from the property – must be enforced. Wynand Venter says Nhleko and Ntlemeza must either give reasons in a court for their conduct, or report to the Pretoria Central Police Station to be arrested. The company will also ask the court to imprison the two in accordance with a contempt order and ask for a costs order against the police, as well as against Nhleko and Ntlemeza personally. According to Venter, the police failed in their constitutional duty to protect the state and its citizens and their interests, as well as their duty to prevent criminal activity that strips the land of its mineral riches. It is probably the biggest, most blatant illegal mining going on in SA today (maybe diamonds come close) and they are stripping the easy shallow chrome away which means these mines will not be economic for a proper mining company to come in later.
